headline: Researchers report that deaths among high-risk hospital patients were lower after 11 hospitals began using an AI risk score to alert rapid response teams automatically.
score_reason: Pool score 6 kept: a large study with clear numbers, but a before-and-after design with stated limits.
importance_line: High-risk hospital patients and the nurses and doctors who respond to emergencies are affected, but the study only compared two time periods, only 46.6% of stays after the change produced an alert, and the results may not carry over to other hospitals.
summary: 2 Minute Medicine reports on a study by Nahass and colleagues at 11 hospital sites, where in-hospital deaths among high-risk adults were 18.6% after an AI warning score began alerting rapid response teams automatically, down from 23.1% before. This was a before-and-after comparison, not a randomised trial, and the report lists unequal seasons and an incomplete roll-out at two hospitals as limits.
notes: The article does not name the journal or give the study's publication date, so freshness is taken from the 3 Oct 2026 summary. Observational design: the drop is an association, not proof the alerts caused it.
